To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the rudder and lid cleft loops are required for promoter recruitment and elongation, that bubble reclosure in the open complex is required for RNA synthesis, and that the archaeal subunit P is required for promoter recruitment.

the rudder, lid, and fork 2 loops of the active site cleft are required for transcription, the rudder for open complex formation; bubble reclosure is a key step for RNA displacement during transcription; TFE is required for open complex formation and is present in elongation, and the P and H subunits of RNAP are not required for RNPA assembly, but are essential for transcription.
the cleft loops are involved in promoter recognition, bubble reclosure and RNA displacement and that the subunits H and P are involved in promoter recruitment and bubble reclosure, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms underlying transcription initiation and elongation in archaea.
the elucidation of the structure-function relationship of RNAP and the transcriptional apparatus of archaea and their eukaryotic orthologues.
the elucidation of the molecular mechanisms of transcription in archaea, and provides a basis for the development of novel antiviral strategies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
archaeal transcription is more similar to bacterial than to eukaryal transcription.
archaeal RNAP is a very versatile and powerful model system for analyses of transcriptional machinery in general.

the archaeal RNAP is the most suitable system for the analysis of eukaryal RNA polymerase II, but that it is also a very useful system for the analysis and comparison with bacterial and eukaryotic RNA polymerases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the archaeal transcriptional machinery can be used as a model system for eukaryotic systems, but the detailed molecular mechanisms of transcription initiation and elongation in eukaryotes are still poorly understood.
the archaeal RNAP can be used as a model to investigate the eukaryal transcriptional machinery and that the eukaryotical RNAP can be reconstituted from archaeal subunits.
the cleft loops in RNAP are essential for transcription and the rudder is required for open complex formation; the rudder, lid, fork 2, P and H are required for promoter-directed transcription.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the archaeal transcriptional machinery is highly conserved, but that it is more modular than previously anticipated.
the archaeal transcription system is a valuable model system for studies of transcriptional regulation in eukaryotes.
archaeal RNAP can be used to study the structure and function of multisubunit eukaryotic polymerases and that the eukaryal polymerases can be used as a tool to study archaeal transcription.
